_comment: Review decisions for the BLFS subset, applied by bin/extract-blfs.py.
Same contract as recipes/review-overrides.json: drop / replace / enable / defer.
BLFS pages carry far more optional and alternative commands than LFS, and mark
root-only commands with <pre class="root">, which is where every 'make install' lives.

2.reason: The page is 'Which-2.23 and Alternatives'. This block is the alternative: 'The second option (for those who don't want to install the package) is to create a simple script'. We install the real package in blocks 0-1, so running this would overwrite the just-installed /usr/bin/which binary with a shell script.
Installs the GTK-Doc API documentation ('If you did not pass --enable-gtk-doc ... you can install the API documentation'). GTK-Doc is not installed and the docs are not needed.

Book uses 'make-ca -g', which downloads certdata.txt from Mozilla at build time. We supply certdata.txt as a verified build input instead (staged in /sources), so the cert store is deterministic and the build needs no network. Note make-ca downloads via 'openssl s_client', not wget/curl, so -g will still work on the booted system.

3.reason: 'systemctl enable' cannot run in the chroot ('System has not been booted with systemd as init system'). Creating the WantedBy=timers.target symlink by hand is exactly what enable would do. This is worth keeping enabled: make-ca fetches via openssl s_client, so the weekly refresh works on the booted system with no extra packages.

4.reason: Optional: adds the CAcert roots, which are not in Mozilla's store. Also fetches them with wget, which is not installed.

5.reason: The book's worked example of distrusting a CA, operating on /etc/ssl/certs/Makebelieve_CA_Root.pem -- a fictional certificate that does not exist. Would fail immediately.

6.reason: A bare 'export _PIP_STANDALONE_CERT=...' illustrating the variable. Setting it inside a build script has no lasting effect; block 7 is the persistent version and is kept.

3.reason: The book appends 'PermitRootLogin no', which is the right default on a system with normal user accounts. This system has only root, so 'no' would make sshd unreachable and defeat the purpose of installing it. Set to 'yes' deliberately and flagged in the build report: change the root password on first boot and move to key-only auth.

4.reason: Interactive 'ssh-keygen' followed by 'ssh-copy-id ... REMOTE_USERNAME@REMOTE_HOSTNAME' -- literal placeholders, and it would block on a prompt.

5.reason: Appends 'PasswordAuthentication no' and 'KbdInteractiveAuthentication no', i.e. key-only auth. No authorized_keys exists on this system, so applying it together with the block above would leave no way to log in at all.

6.reason: Builds /etc/pam.d/sshd from /etc/pam.d/login. Linux-PAM is not part of LFS 13.0 and Shadow was built without it, so /etc/pam.d/login does not exist and the sed would fail.

7.reason: 'make install-sshd' is a target of the blfs-systemd-units package, not of openssh's own Makefile -- the book shows it under 'Systemd Unit' referring to blfs-systemd-units-20251204. Running it in the openssh tree fails. Handled instead by the blfs-sshd-unit step.

1.reason: The book's configure line passes --shared-brotli, --shared-cares, --shared-libuv, --shared-nghttp2 and --with-intl=system-icu, because BLFS assumes you installed those 'recommended' dependencies. We deliberately did not: Node bundles all of them, and using the bundled copies keeps the dependency closure to the one package Node actually requires (which). Configure would fail outright looking for the missing system libraries. --shared-openssl and --shared-zlib are kept because LFS provides both (OpenSSL 3.6.1, zlib 1.3.2), so Node benefits from system security updates rather than carrying its own copy.
'make html' builds the HTML docs and requires asciidoc, which is not installed. The book gates it on 'If you have installed asciidoc'.

2.reason: 'make man' builds the man pages and requires both asciidoc and xmlto, neither installed. We use the prebuilt git-manpages tarball instead (block 6).

4.reason: 'make install-man' installs man pages built by block 2. Since we do not build them, there is nothing to install and the target would fail.

5.reason: 'make install-html' installs HTML docs built by block 1. Same reason: not built, so nothing to install.

7.reason: Untars git-htmldocs-2.53.0.tar.xz, which we deliberately did not download -- HTML documentation is not wanted and the tarball is large. The book presents it as an alternative to block 1/5, not an addition.

8.reason: Reorganises the HTML doc tree that block 7 would have unpacked. With block 7 dropped the paths do not exist and the mv commands would fail.

2.reason: 'make -C doc pdf && make -C doc ps', gated on 'If you have texlive-20250308 installed'. texlive is not installed.

4.reason: Installs the pdf/ps/dvi docs built by block 2. Not built, so nothing to install and the install would fail.

2.cmd:
install -v -dm755 /etc/systemd/scripts

cat > /etc/systemd/scripts/iptables << "EOF"
#!/bin/sh

# Begin /etc/systemd/scripts/iptables

# Insert connection-tracking modules
# (not needed if built into the kernel)
modprobe nf_conntrack
modprobe xt_LOG

# Enable broadcast echo Protection
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts

# Disable Source Routed Packets
echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/accept_source_route
echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/default/accept_source_route

# Enable TCP SYN Cookie Protection
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_syncookies

# Disable ICMP Redirect Acceptance
echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/default/accept_redirects

# Do not send Redirect Messages
echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/send_redirects
echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/default/send_redirects

# Drop Spoofed Packets coming in on an interface, where responses
# would result in the reply going out a different interface.
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/rp_filter
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/default/rp_filter

# Log packets with impossible addresses.
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/all/log_martians
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/conf/default/log_martians

# be verbose on dynamic ip-addresses  (not needed in case of static IP)
echo 2 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_dynaddr

# disable Explicit Congestion Notification
# too many routers are still ignorant
echo 0 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/tcp_ecn

# Set a known state
iptables -P INPUT   DROP
iptables -P FORWARD DROP
iptables -P OUTPUT  DROP

# These lines are here in case rules are already in place and the
# script is ever rerun on the fly. We want to remove all rules and
# pre-existing user defined chains before we implement new rules.
iptables -F
iptables -X
iptables -Z

iptables -t nat -F

# Allow local-only connections
iptables -A INPUT  -i lo -j ACCEPT

# Free output on any interface to any ip for any service
# (equal to -P ACCEPT)
iptables -A OUTPUT -j ACCEPT

# Permit answers on already established connections
# and permit new connections related to established ones
# (e.g. port mode ftp)
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT

# Not in the book's example: this box is administered entirely over SSH, and
# the book's own Personal Firewall script does not allow any inbound service,
# SSH included -- applying it unmodified would have locked out the only way
# in. Explicit allow for new inbound SSH connections; the ESTABLISHED,RELATED
# rule above already covers the rest of each session once it exists.
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j ACCEPT

# Everything else is dropped by policy (no LOG rule -- the book's example logs
# every dropped packet, which on an internet-facing host is a constant stream
# of scan/noise traffic; not wanted here, dropped without a paper trail).

# End /etc/systemd/scripts/iptables
EOF
chmod 700 /etc/systemd/scripts/iptables
2.reason: Book's 'Personal Firewall' example (single-interface, matches this box) with two changes: an explicit ACCEPT for new inbound SSH (tcp/22) before the closing rule -- the book's own script allows no inbound service at all, which would have locked out the only access path to this machine -- and the book's final 'LOG everything else' rule dropped entirely (operator's call: never going to review the log, and on an internet-facing host it's a constant stream of scan noise). Everything else is the book's text unchanged.

3.reason: The 'Masquerading Router' example -- two network interfaces (LAN1/WAN1), NAT/routing between them. This box has one NIC (enp6s0) and is a single server, not a router; the block references interface names that do not exist here.

x11_backend and wayland_backend pinned explicitly rather than left on meson's auto default (rebuilt 2026-08-27 after a real failure). Auto silently enabled the Wayland backend because wayland happened to be installed at the time, and that made gdk-3.0.pc unconditionally declare Requires: wayland-client, wayland-cursor, wayland-egl. Removing the wayland package later -- correctly, nothing here used it -- broke `pkg-config gtk+-3.0` for every consumer, Firefox's configure included, even though nothing ever used gtk3's Wayland backend. The lesson is not about Wayland: a backend left on auto encodes whatever was present at build time into the installed .pc file. Declare both. A host that does run Wayland should override this block with wayland_backend=true rather than reverting to auto.
